# Joshua 3: research notes, verse by verse

**Gaps to know about first:**
- I didn't find any NET Bible translator notes, and nothing on oca.org.
- I didn't find any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so that part is left out.
- Studylight lists Wesley's Notes for v. 16, but I didn't read what they say.
- I found almost no real disagreement *between* Protestant traditions. The main debate is *how far to take the symbolism*, and it cuts across traditions (see the debates section near the end).

---

## The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:**
- Guzik says this was the last stage of the journey from Egypt. The Jordan was the final obstacle before the Promised Land. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- Matthew Henry reads Joshua's early rising as a sign that he cared more about his work than his comfort. He adds that "Those that would bring great tings to pass must rise early." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_003.cfm
- John J. Davis sees Joshua's speed as proof that he trusted God. He didn't ask for time to let the river go down, or look for another route. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary
- George Bush points out that nothing says the people were told *how* they would cross. They went forward in faith anyway. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary

**v. 2:**
- Guzik: the people camped for three days within sight of a river swollen by spring rain. One person could swim it at flood time, but only as a heroic act. A whole nation with children and animals could not. God gave them three days to think about the problem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- Blaikie: the three days were for moral and spiritual preparation, perhaps more than physical. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary

**v. 3:**
- Guzik: Joshua sent the priests with the ark first, not engineers. That made this a spiritual challenge before it was a building problem. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- Guzik also notes that the Kohathites normally carried the ark. Priests carried it only on special occasions such as this one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- Henry stresses the phrase "the LORD *your* God": the people were in covenant with Him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_003.cfm

**v. 4:**
- Guzik gives two reasons for the gap of about 1,000 yards (2,000 cubits):
  - to respect the ark's holiness;
  - so the whole nation could see the ark and follow it.
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- BibleHub's chapter summary gives the distance as about two-thirds of a mile and links it to God's holiness. https://biblehub.com/joshua/3.htm
- Henry applies "you have never traveled this way before" to life generally, including the way through death. If God is present, there is no need to fear. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_003.cfm

**v. 5:**
- "Consecrate yourselves" means setting yourself apart from ordinary things to focus on the Lord (Guzik).
- Adam Clarke, quoted by Guzik, thinks it probably meant the same as Exodus 19:10–14: washing themselves and their clothes before God acted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- George Bush agrees that it matches Moses' command before Sinai. He suggests the order was actually given the day before. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary
- Henry (Concise): if we want to see God's love and power at work, we must put away sin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary

**v. 6:**
- Guzik: this wasn't recklessness. God had told Joshua what to do, and Joshua remembered the Red Sea. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik, points out that Psalm 114 puts the Red Sea and the Jordan crossing side by side. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- Precept Austin calls this a "crisis of faith." As far as the text shows, the priests didn't know their steps would dry up the river. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary

**v. 7:**
- Guzik: God encourages people in the things He commands them to do. Here He promises to make Joshua a leader like Moses, through a water crossing like the Red Sea. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- Henry: God honours Joshua, and Joshua in turn honours God. Henry also notes that the Aramaic paraphrase (Targum) reads "the Word of the Lord," which he takes as the eternal Word. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_003.cfm
- George Bush thinks God probably spoke these words *before* the orders in vv. 5–6. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary

**v. 8:**
- Guzik: the priests were to step into the edge of the water, then stop and stand there holding the ark. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/

**v. 9:**
- Guzik: Joshua puts the emphasis on God's word; he is only the messenger.
- John Trapp, quoted by Guzik, says miracles are like bells calling people to the sermon. Faith itself comes by hearing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- Henry: hear the words first, so you can compare them with the works. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_003.cfm

**v. 10:**
- Guzik: the crossing would confirm that God was with them for the whole conquest.
- He quotes David Howard: seven nations are listed here, probably standing for completeness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- Donald Campbell calls "the living God is among you" the watchword of the conquest. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary
- Precept Austin notes that Joshua didn't pass on God's private promise to exalt *him*. It reads that as humility. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary

**v. 11:**
- Guzik: sending priests ahead instead of soldiers showed that victory would be spiritual, not military.
- He quotes Francis Schaeffer: the ark was not an image of God but a statement of God's character. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/

**v. 12:**
- The commentaries I read mostly tie the twelve men to the memorial stones in chapter 4.
- Gregory of Nyssa sees the twelve stones as pointing ahead to the twelve disciples, "the ministers of Baptism." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/2910.htm

**v. 13:**
- Guzik: the waters would be cut off upstream, not divided as at the Red Sea. God's work is the same in some ways and new in others.
- He also quotes Richard Hess. Earthquakes in the Jordan valley are known to block the river, but the text mentions none. Whatever the secondary causes, the point is to exalt God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- Precept Austin: God acted only after the priests obeyed. It adds that if God isn't acting for you, you may not have obeyed far enough. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary

**v. 14:**
- Precept Austin: the people showed faith by breaking camp toward a river still in flood. The priests showed faith by getting their feet wet. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary

**v. 15:**
- Guzik: the text doesn't say how long the priests stood in the water before it stopped. People naturally want the riverbed dry before they step in. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- Adam Clarke, quoted by Guzik, explains the flood: snow melting on Lebanon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- Bob Utley (bible.org) says this was the flax and barley harvest, with meltwater from Mount Hermon, when crossing was almost impossible. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-3
- Ligonier adds that the banks would have been thick with brambles. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/israel-crosses-jordan-river

**v. 16:**
- **The text itself.** The written Hebrew says "*in* Adam"; the Jewish scribes' marginal reading says "*from* Adam."
  - Ellicott (Anglican) says the meaning is the same either way, and the harder reading, "in," may be original. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/joshua-3.html
  - Keil & Delitzsch say "in" should not be changed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/3-16.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary calls the scribes' correction unnecessary. It also notes that the wording here turns poetic, like Exodus 15:8. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/3-16.htm
- **Where Adam was.**
  - Gill (Baptist) places Adam on the east bank and Zaretan on the west. He takes "beside Zaretan" to describe the heap of water, not the city. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/3-16.html
  - Barnes (Presbyterian) links Zarthan to Kurn Sartabeh, a lone hill about 17 miles upriver from Jericho. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/3-16.htm
  - Hess, quoted by Guzik, identifies Adam with Tell ed-Damiye, 18 miles north of Jericho. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- **How it happened.**
  - Guzik allows that God may have used an earthquake or landslide. He cites recorded blockages in A.D. 1267 and 1927 near Adam. Even so, the *timing* was a miracle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
  - Bible.org mentions the same landslides but gives garbled dates ("1267 b.c." and "a.d. 1297"). Guzik's dates look more reliable. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-3
  - Coffman notes that Adam sits beside the tallest mud cliffs on the Jordan's banks. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/3-16.html
  - Matthew Poole argues that if pagan writers credited magicians with such things, it is shameless to doubt God's power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/3-16.htm
  - Poole also suggests God brought them over opposite Jericho because it was the strongest point and the most fertile land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/3-16.htm

**v. 17:**
- Utley: in v. 15 the priests stood at the edge; by v. 17 they seem to have moved to the middle of the river. https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-3
- Henry: stepping in was bold, and standing longest in the middle was bolder still, but they carried their protection with them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jos/Jos_003.cfm
- Ligonier quotes Henry: repeating the Red Sea miracle shows God can finish his people's salvation as surely as He began it. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/israel-crosses-jordan-river
- Guzik: the riverbed was dry, solid ground rather than mud. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/

---

## Where Protestant teachers differ

**Whole chapter (and vv. 15–16): how much symbolism to see**
- **Spurgeon (Baptist)** grants that reading the crossing as a picture of death and entering heaven is an imperfect type. But it is long established in the church and has helped believers, so he uses it. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons34/sermons34.xxxvii.html
- **Precept Austin (evangelical)** rejects that heaven reading, taken from the Treasury of Scripture Knowledge. Israel entered a sinful land full of war, and heaven has neither. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary
- **Scofield and J. Vernon McGee (dispensational)** see the crossing as a picture of death with Christ. McGee even reads the town of Adam as pointing back to the first man (v. 16). Precept Austin thinks this goes too far, though it admits it could be wrong. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary
- **Wiersbe** takes a middle line. The Red Sea pictures leaving the old life; the Jordan pictures entering by faith into our inheritance in Christ, won one battle at a time. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary
- **Paul Apple** reads the chapter as moving from defeated self-effort to the victorious life of faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary

**v. 5: does God's act depend on the people?**
- G. Campbell Morgan, quoted by Guzik, says the act was wholly God's, but the people's consecration made it "possible." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-3/
- Wayne Barber says God removed the barrier "only when" the people consecrated themselves and focused on Him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/Joshua-sermons-joshua1-6-wayne-barber
- Henry puts it more as a call to put away sin. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-3-commentary

**Lutheran: a baptism reading**
- A 1517.org article lists Joshua 3 among Old Testament pictures of baptism. It quotes Cyril of Jerusalem: Joshua took command at the Jordan just as Christ began his ministry after being baptized. https://www.1517.org/articles/baptism-foreshadowed-in-old-testament-narratives
- Another 1517.org writer calls Jesus both the ark and the "new Joshua," bringing us into the Father's kingdom. https://www.1517.org/articles/the-hebrew-stories-swimming-beneath-jesuss-baptism

---

## Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- Bible Odyssey says Joshua "claims" this crossing happened. It suggests the Jordan may play a bigger part in the Bible's stories than it did in actual history, and that the conquest story became central to Israel's identity. https://en.bibleodyssey.org/articles/the-jordan-river-in-israelite-history/
- It also describes crossing the Jordan as a key theme in how Israel understood itself. Later, African American spirituals used it as a picture of liberation. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/jordan-river/

**Catholic and early Church readings**
- Catholic.com says some Church Fathers, such as Gregory and Augustine, read the turning back of the waters as a picture of baptism. In baptism a person returns to the origin they had strayed from. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/joshua
- Gregory of Nyssa says the Hebrews entered the promised land only after crossing the Jordan with Joshua as guide. To him the Jordan is uniquely the river of baptism's grace. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/2910.htm
- Origen says the Joshua crossing points to Christian truths and was written to instruct us. https://biblehub.com/library/origen/origens_commentary_on_the_gospel_of_john/26_the_story_of_israel.htm
- Haydock's Catholic commentary (v. 16) has the water rolling back almost to the Sea of Galilee, about twenty leagues above Jericho. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/3-16.html
